summary_grc: οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι τῷ λιμῷ ἀπολλύμενοι τὴν εἰρήνην δέχονται, καὶ τὰ τείχη κατασκάπτεται ὑπʼ αὐλητρίδων.
summary_en: 404 BC: blockaded and starving, Athens sends Theramenes to Sparta. The terms: pull down the Long Walls, hand over the fleet, take back the exiles, follow Sparta by land and sea. The Assembly accepts, and the walls come down to the music of flute-girls. Xenophon, Hellenica 2.2.20–23, unadapted, with a short frame: ἐφʼ ᾧ + infinitive, fear clauses, ἔδοξε.
caption_grc: καὶ τὰ τείχη κατέσκαπτον ὑπʼ αὐλητρίδων πολλῇ προθυμίᾳ.

original.note: Xenophon, Hellenica 2.2.20–23, uncut. The first two sentences are ours: they borrow Xenophon's own words for the night the Paralus brought the news (2.2.3) and summarise the siege (2.2.10–19). The peace was accepted in spring 404 BC.

grammar.md:
**Reading a treaty.** Greek historians report terms of peace in a fixed pattern, and once you know it the longest sentence in this lesson is easy.

**1. ἐφʼ ᾧ + infinitive 'on condition that'.** The terms depend on one infinitive (ἕπεσθαι), and the other obligations are packed into participles that agree with its (unexpressed) subject, the Athenians, in the **accusative**:

> ἐποιοῦντο εἰρήνην ἐφʼ ᾧ
> — τά τε μακρὰ τείχη καὶ τὸν Πειραιᾶ **καθελόντας** (having pulled down)
> — καὶ τὰς ναῦς πλὴν δώδεκα **παραδόντας** (having handed over)
> — καὶ τοὺς φυγάδας **καθέντας** (having let back)
> — τὸν αὐτὸν ἐχθρὸν καὶ φίλον **νομίζοντας** (considering)
> — Λακεδαιμονίοις **ἕπεσθαι** … ὅποι ἂν ἡγῶνται. (to follow wherever they lead)

**2. Reported speech after a past verb (9.3–9.4).** ἀπήγγελλον ἐφʼ οἷς … **ποιοῖντο** (indirect question, optative); φοβούμενοι μὴ … **ἥκοιεν** (fear clause, optative); λέγων ὡς **χρή** (indirect statement, the indicative kept).

**3. How the Assembly decides.** The debate in genitive absolutes (ἀντειπόντων τινων … πλειόνων συνεπαινεσάντων), the result in the decree formula **ἔδοξε** + infinitive: 'it was resolved to accept the peace'. Inscribed decrees begin ἔδοξε τῇ βουλῇ καὶ τῷ δήμῳ.

**4. The historian's irony.** The last sentence reports what the victors thought (νομίζοντες …): that the fall of Athens was the first day of freedom for Greece. Xenophon, writing after Sparta's own harsh rule, does not comment.

culture.title: The fall of Athens, 404 BC
culture.md:
After Aegospotami Athens had no fleet and could not bring in grain. Lysander sailed round the Aegean restoring the exiled oligarchs of Athens' allies and sending every Athenian he found back to the city, to eat its food; the Spartan kings camped in the Academy and Lysander's fleet shut Piraeus. Through the winter of 405/404 people died of hunger. **Theramenes** spent three months with Lysander, then went to Sparta.

Corinth and Thebes wanted Athens destroyed and its people sold, as Athens had done to Melos and Scione. Sparta refused, because of what Athens had done for Greece against Persia. The terms: the **Long Walls** and the walls of Piraeus pulled down, all but **twelve ships** handed over, the **exiles** (mostly oligarchs) allowed back, and Athens to have the same friends and enemies as Sparta and follow wherever Sparta led.

In spring 404 the Assembly accepted. Lysander sailed in, and the walls were pulled down 'to the music of flute-girls', the Peloponnesians believing that 'that day was the beginning of freedom for Greece'. Within months the returned exiles had set up the **Thirty** (hist.6). The walls were rebuilt by Conon, with Persian money, in 394–391. Stretches of the Themistoclean city wall can still be seen in the Kerameikos, next to the Dipylon Gate.
